al-jabr.role: a young copyist at the House of Wisdom
goals: Turn a problem written in words into an equation
Solve \(x^2 + bx = c\) by *completing the square*, and see why it works
Know what *al-jabr* and *al-muqābala* mean, and where the words *algebra* and *algorithm* come from

sources.title: Rosen, F. (1831). The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa (the full translation, scanned at the Internet Archive)
Wikipedia: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing

map.caption: The Round City of Baghdad was founded in 762 on the Tigris. The dashed line follows the Khurasan Road east through Rayy, Nishapur and Merv, then down the Amu Darya to Khwarazm, the oasis al-Khwarizmi's family name points to.

steps.text: The Round City is barely sixty years old. Barges crowd the Tigris, and the markets sell paper, a material still new here. You work as *a young copyist* for the caliph al-Ma'mūn, in the palace library people call the *House of Wisdom*.

picture.caption: Morning on the Tigris. Across the water are the brick walls of the Round City and, at its centre, the Green Dome of the caliph's palace: about 48 m high, with a statue of a horseman holding a lance on top. A round kuphar and a sailing barge work the river. (A reconstruction.)

steps.text: All day, scholars around you translate books from Greek, Persian and Sanskrit into Arabic, and you copy their work neatly onto fresh sheets. This morning you are given a different job: copying a new book by one of the court's own scholars.

steps.caption: The palace library. Scholars read and translate; you copy, writing on a board on your knee. (A reconstruction: no picture of the House of Wisdom survives.)

steps.name: Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī
steps.bio: Astronomer and mathematician at the court of al-Ma'mūn. His family name points to Khwarazm, a region south of the Aral Sea.

steps.text: His book is not for scholars alone. He says so in its first pages: it is for the problems ordinary people meet every day.

…what is easiest and most useful in arithmetic, such as men constantly require in cases of inheritance, legacies, partition, law-suits, and trade, and in all their dealings with one another, or where the measuring of lands, the digging of canals, geometrical computation, and other objects of various sorts and kinds are concerned.
A problem made of words

There are no symbols in the book: no \(x\), no \(=\), no \(+\). Everything is written in words. He uses three kinds of quantity: the *root* (the unknown number), the *square* (the root times itself), and plain numbers, which he counts in *dirhams*, the silver coin in your purse.
One square, and ten roots of the same, amount to thirty-nine dirhems; that is to say, what must be the square which, when increased by ten of its own roots, amounts to thirty-nine?

steps.then: One square, and ten roots of the same, amount to thirty-nine dirhems.
steps.note: \(x\) is the root, \(x^2\) the square, \(10x\) is ten roots.

steps.prompt: How would you write *“a square and four roots are equal to twenty-one”* in modern symbols?
steps.why: *A square* is \(x^2\), *four roots* is \(4x\), and the plain number 21 goes on the other side. (The answer is \(x = 3\): \(9 + 12 = 21\).)

steps.prompt: Before learning his method, try guessing. Which whole number \(x\) makes \(x^2 + 10x = 39\) true?
hints: Try \(x = 4\): \(16 + 40 = 56\). Too big. So the answer is between 2 and 4.

mistakes.say: Check it: \(16 + 40 = 56\), which is more than 39.
Check it: \(4 + 20 = 24\), which is less than 39.

steps.text: Guessing works when the answer is a small whole number. But the next problem might have an answer like \(2.4\), or \(1\tfrac{3}{8}\) of a field. A merchant or a judge dividing an inheritance needs a method that works *every* time. That is what al-Khwarizmi gives.
Completing the square

His trick is to stop thinking of \(x^2 + 10x\) as numbers and start thinking of it as *shapes*. A square is a square: \(x\) by \(x\). Ten roots is a rectangle, \(10\) by \(x\). Together their area is 39.
Now the same steps as arithmetic. Each line follows from the one before.

lines.why: add the missing \(5 \times 5\) corner to both sides
the left side is now a complete square, with side \(x + 5\)
the side of a square with area 64 is 8

notebook.title: Completing the square
notebook.text: To solve \(x^2 + bx = c\): halve \(b\), square it, add it to both sides, take the square root, then subtract half of \(b\).

steps.text: Here is how he tells it in the book. This is the same recipe, in words:

The solution is this: you halve the number of the roots, which in the present instance yields five. This you multiply by itself; the product is twenty-five. Add this to thirty-nine; the sum is sixty-four. Now take the root of this, which is eight, and subtract from it half the number of the roots, which is five; the remainder is three. This is the root of the square which you sought for; the square itself is nine.

steps.label: The recipe
steps.text: *Halve* the roots → *square* it → *add* it to the number → take the *root* → *subtract* the half.

steps.prompt: Your turn. *A square and six roots are equal to sixteen*: \(x^2 + 6x = 16\). Use the recipe. What is the root \(x\)?
hints: Halve the roots: half of 6 is 3. Square it: 9.
Add: \(16 + 9 = 25\). The root of 25 is 5. Now subtract the half.

mistakes.say: 5 is \(x + 3\), the side of the big square. Subtract the half (3) to get \(x\).
\(-8\) does make the equation true, but al-Khwarizmi only accepts positive answers. More on that soon.
Check it: \(16 + 24 = 40\), not 16. Did you add 9 to 16 before taking the root?

steps.text: Restoring and balancing

The book's title names two moves that tidy an equation before the recipe can start. *Al-jabr* means *restoring*: when something is subtracted on one side, you add it back to both sides so nothing is missing. *Al-muqābala* means *balancing*: when the same kind of thing appears on both sides, you take away the smaller amount from both.

stages.caption: One square equals forty roots minus four squares. Something is missing on the right.
Five squares equal forty roots, so one square equals eight roots and the root is 8.
Fifty and a square equal twenty-nine and ten roots. There are plain numbers on both sides.
A square and twenty-one equal ten roots.

steps.label: From the book
steps.text: Both examples come from worked problems in al-Khwarizmi's book. (Rosen's 1831 translation calls the two moves *completion* and *reduction*.) The Arabic word *al-jabr* was also used for setting a broken bone. Latin translators kept it, and it became our word *algebra*.

steps.why: Restoring adds back what was subtracted: the \(-2x\) becomes \(+2x\) on the other side. Taking 8 from both sides is balancing (*al-muqābala*). Dividing by 2 is a third move he calls reducing.

steps.text: Two answers

The equation from the second balance, *a square and twenty-one equal ten roots*, is a different shape of problem: \(x^2 + 21 = 10x\). Here al-Khwarizmi notices something new. The recipe can end in two ways: you may subtract the root from the half, or add it.

Or you may add the root to the moiety of the roots; the sum is seven; this is the root of the square which you sought for, and the square itself is forty-nine. When you meet with an instance which refers you to this case, try its solution by addition, and if that do not serve, then subtraction certainly will.
steps.cite: al-Khwarizmi, tr. F. Rosen (1831). (“Moiety” means half.)

steps.prompt: Solve \(x^2 + 21 = 10x\) with his steps: halve the roots (5), square it (25), *subtract* 21, take the root, then subtract it from 5, or add it to 5. Enter both answers, separated by a comma.
hints: \(25 - 21 = 4\), and the root of 4 is 2.

mistakes.say: 3 works. There is a second answer: add the 2 to 5 as well.
7 works. There is a second answer: subtract the 2 from 5 as well.

steps.label: Why only positive answers?
steps.text: Al-Khwarizmi works without negative numbers. A root is a length or an amount of money, so it can't be less than nothing. That is also why he needs *six* separate kinds of equation instead of one: he can't write \(x^2 - 10x + 21 = 0\), because nothing may be subtracted. When the numbers make the root impossible (if 21 were bigger than 25), he says plainly that the question is impossible.

steps.caption: Late afternoon in the library, with the lamp lit. (A reconstruction.)

lines.narration: Late in the afternoon, al-Khwarizmi stops beside you to check the copy.

lines.text: You have copied the rule. Can you use it? A square and eight roots are equal to thirty-three. Where do you begin?
I halve the roots. Half of eight is four.
wrong: I take the root of thirty-three.

lines.text: Four times itself is sixteen. I add it to thirty-three and get forty-nine.
wrong: Four times itself is sixteen. I take it from thirty-three and get seventeen.

lines.text: What is the root of forty-nine?
Seven. I take away the half, four, and the root is three.
wrong: Seven, and that is the root we want.
Seven. I add the four, and the root is eleven.

lines.text: Nine. Nine and eight roots, twenty-four, make thirty-three.
wrong: Three. The square and the root are the same.

lines.narration: He nods and moves on to the next copyist.

steps.text: What happened next

The book spread across the Islamic world, and in 1145 Robert of Chester translated it into Latin in Spain as *Liber algebrae et almucabola*. Europe took the word *al-jabr* as the name of the whole subject: *algebra*. Another of al-Khwarizmi's books, on calculating with the Indian digits 0 to 9, was translated as *Algoritmi de numero Indorum*, “al-Khwarizmi on the Indian numbers”. His name became the word *algorithm*.

Two centuries earlier, Brahmagupta had written a rule for solving the same kind of equation, and he was willing to work with negative numbers (“debts”). Al-Khwarizmi's contribution was to make the method systematic, explain it with geometry, and write it for everyday use.

steps.label: Legend or history?
steps.text: The House of Wisdom is often pictured as a grand university. Historians such as Dimitri Gutas argue it was mainly a palace library and translation office; the translation movement was much wider than one building. And the title “father of algebra” is shared: many historians give it to Diophantus, whose *Arithmetica* came five centuries earlier.

One kind of problem still resisted him: equations with a *cube* in them, such as \(x^3 + 2x = 12\). A cube is a solid, and completing a square won't finish it. Two and a half centuries later, a poet-astronomer in Isfahan took up that challenge (*Cubics from cones*).
Echoes today

steps.title: A frame with an even border
steps.text: You have a 20 cm × 30 cm print and a frame whose total area is 1,200 cm². How wide is the border, if it is the same width \(w\) all round? The framed size is \((20 + 2w)(30 + 2w) = 1200\). Multiplying out and dividing by 4 gives \(w^2 + 25w = 150\): a square and twenty-five roots equal a hundred and fifty.

problem.prompt: Solve \(w^2 + 25w = 150\) with the recipe. How wide is the border, in cm?

mistakes.say: 17.5 is \(w + 12.5\). Subtract the half.

steps.title: When does the fountain's water reach 15 m?
steps.text: A fountain shoots water straight up at 20 m/s. Taking gravity as 10 m/s² to keep the numbers simple, its height after \(t\) seconds is \(h = 20t - 5t^2\). Setting \(h = 15\) and dividing by 5 gives \(t^2 + 3 = 4t\): al-Khwarizmi's fifth kind, squares and numbers equal roots. Like his \(x^2 + 21 = 10x\), it has two answers.

problem.prompt: Solve \(t^2 + 3 = 4t\). Enter both times, in seconds, separated by a comma.
hints: Halve the roots: 2. Square it: 4. Subtract 3: 1.
The root of 1 is 1. Now \(2 - 1\) and \(2 + 1\).

mistakes.say: 1 s is on the way up. The water passes 15 m again on the way down.
3 s is on the way down. It also passes 15 m on the way up.

steps.title: Every app runs on algorithms
steps.text: An *algorithm* is a recipe of exact steps that always works, which is exactly what al-Khwarizmi wrote. The steps you've learned (halve, square, add, root, subtract) could be typed into a spreadsheet or a program without changing a word. Your phone's calculator, a map app's route and a bank's interest calculation are all algorithms.

problem.prompt: Run the algorithm on \(x^2 + 4x = 60\). What is \(x\)?
hints: Half of 4 is 2, squared is 4. \(60 + 4 = 64\).

mistakes.say: 8 is \(x + 2\). Subtract the half.

khwarizmi.note: A pixel figure, not a likeness: no portrait of him survives. He is drawn in a turban and a dark outer robe, since black was the colour of the Abbasid dynasty he served.

earth.role: a young assistant at the Library of Alexandria
goals: Treat an angle as a fraction of a full turn
Use parallel lines and *alternate angles* to carry an angle from a shadow to the Earth's centre
Scale a small arc up to a whole circle, and judge how accurate the answer is

sources.title: Heath, T. L. (1921). A History of Greek Mathematics, vol. II, pp. 106–108 (public domain, Internet Archive)
Heath, T. L. (1913). Aristarchus of Samos, pp. 147–148 (public domain, Internet Archive)

eratosthenes.note: A pixel figure, not a likeness: no reliable portrait of him survives. He is drawn in a knee-length chiton with a himation cloak over the left shoulder, as Greek men of his time wore them.

picture.caption: Morning in the harbour of Alexandria. Across the water, the Lighthouse on Pharos island: three tiers of pale stone (square, eight-sided, round) with a fire at the top. It had been finished only a few decades earlier, under Ptolemy II. (A reconstruction.)

map.caption: Syene, today's Aswan, lies far up the Nile, 5,000 stades south of Alexandria by the reckoning of the day (about 800 km). Eratosthenes grew up in Cyrene, to the west.

steps.text: Alexandria is not yet a hundred years old, and ships from all over the Mediterranean crowd its harbour. You work as *a young assistant* at the *Library*, part of the royal Museum, where the king pays scholars to read, write and argue.

The Library has a new head. King Ptolemy III has summoned him from Athens, and he is also to tutor the king's son. He writes poetry, history and maps. And he wants to know something nobody has measured well: how big is the Earth?

steps.name: Eratosthenes of Cyrene
steps.bio: Born in Cyrene, in today's Libya. Chief librarian at Alexandria, mathematician, astronomer and poet. He coined the words *geography* and *geographer*.

steps.text: Educated Greeks have known for a century that the Earth is a ball: in an eclipse, its shadow on the Moon is always round (Aristotle's argument). Archimedes mentions an estimate of 300,000 stades around, but nobody trusts it. A *stade* (stadion) is a Greek unit of distance, roughly 150 to 200 m.
A shadow that isn't there

Travellers bring a strange report from Syene, far up the Nile. At noon on the longest day of the year, upright sticks there cast no shadow at all, and the sun shines straight down a deep well, lighting the water at the bottom.

steps.caption: Syene at noon on the longest day (shown cut away). The sun stands almost straight overhead, so the stick casts no shadow and light reaches the water at the bottom of the well. (A reconstruction.)

steps.text: He observed (1) that at Syene, at noon, at the summer solstice, the sun cast no shadow from an upright gnomon (this was confirmed by the observation that a well dug at the same place was entirely lighted up at the same time), while (2) at the same moment the gnomon fixed upright at Alexandria (taken to be on the same meridian with Syene) cast a shadow corresponding to an angle between the gnomon and the sun's rays of 1/50th of a complete circle or four right angles.
steps.cite: T. L. Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics (1921), retelling the account in Cleomedes

steps.text: In Alexandria, at that same noon, a stick *does* cast a short shadow. Eratosthenes measures it in a *skaphe*: a stone bowl carved as a sundial, with a pointer (a *gnomon*) standing up from the bottom, so the shadow's angle can be read straight off the bowl.

steps.caption: Noon in a courtyard of the Museum. The skaphe's pointer throws a short shadow across the bowl, and people cast only small shadows because the sun is nearly overhead. (A reconstruction: no picture of the Library survives.)

sources.title: Heath, T. L. (1913). Aristarchus of Samos, pp. 147–148 (public domain, Internet Archive)

steps.prompt: At the same moment, a stick at Syene casts no shadow but a stick at Alexandria does. Why?
options: The ground is curved, so the two sticks point in slightly different directions
The sun is closer to Syene than to Alexandria
The sun's rays spread out, so they hit Syene straight on and Alexandria at a slant
steps.why: The sun is so far away that its rays arrive parallel. What differs is the ground: on a round Earth, "straight up" at Alexandria is tilted compared with "straight up" at Syene. (The third option is the most common wrong idea: the rays really are parallel.)

steps.text: From a shadow to the whole Earth

steps.prompt: Eratosthenes gave the angle as \(\tfrac{1}{50}\) of a full circle. A full circle is 360°. How many degrees is that?
hints: Divide the whole circle by 50.
\(360 \div 50\): 50 goes into 350 seven times, and 10 is left over.

mistakes.say: 50 is how many times the angle fits in a circle. Divide 360 by 50.
That's \(360 \times 50\). You want one fiftieth of 360, so divide.

lines.why: the same as the shadow angle (alternate angles)
the arc from Syene to Alexandria is the same fraction of the circumference \(C\) as its angle is of a full turn

notebook.title: Measuring a circle from one arc
notebook.text: If an arc of length \(d\) makes an angle \(\theta\) at the centre, the whole circle is \(C = d \times \dfrac{360°}{\theta}\).

steps.prompt: Check the last step yourself: if \(\tfrac{1}{50}\) of the Earth's circumference is 5,000 stades, how many stades is the whole circumference?
hints: One fiftieth of it is 5,000, so the whole is 50 of those.

mistakes.say: That's \(5000 \div 50\). The arc is the small part; the whole circle is 50 times bigger.
Adding doesn't scale it up. You need 50 lots of 5,000.

lines.narration: Noon on the longest day. Eratosthenes crouches by the skaphe and marks the tip of the shadow.

lines.text: There. One fiftieth of the circle of the bowl. And at Syene, right now, there is no shadow at all. What does that tell us?
That the ground here and the ground at Syene point different ways, because the Earth is curved.
wrong: That the sun is nearer to Syene than to us.
That the sun's rays spread out, so they reach Syene straight and us at a slant.

lines.text: Good. Now imagine the two sticks pushed straight down into the Earth. Where do they go?
They meet at the centre, at the same angle: one fiftieth of a circle.
wrong: Nowhere; they are parallel, so they never meet.
They meet at the centre, at an angle of one fifth of a circle.

lines.text: And the road from Syene to here is 5,000 stades. So the whole Earth is…?
Write it down. The king will want to know how big his world is.

steps.text: Was he right?
It depends on the *stade*, and we don't know exactly which one he used: Greek stades ranged from about 155 m to 185 m. Heath, working from Pliny, suggested 157.5 m.

steps.prompt: Using Heath's stade of 157.5 m, how many kilometres is 250,000 stades?
hints: First find metres: \(250\,000 \times 157.5\). The calculator can do the multiplying.
Then divide by 1,000 to get kilometres. (Type Ans ÷ 1000 to reuse your last result.)

mistakes.say: That's in metres. Divide by 1,000 for kilometres.
That divides by 157.5. Each stade is 157.5 m, so multiply.

steps.prompt: The Earth measured over the poles is 40,008 km around. If his stade was the longer 185 m, he would have got \(250\,000 \times 0.185 = 46\,250\) km. By what percentage is that too big?
hints: How much too big is it, in km? \(46\,250 - 40\,008\).
Divide that by the true value, 40,008, and multiply by 100.

mistakes.say: That's the error in km. Turn it into a percentage of 40,008.
That divides by 46,250. Percentage error compares with the true value, 40,008.

solution: With Heath's 157.5 m stade, the answer is only about 1.6% too small.

steps.text: …a surprisingly close approximation, however much it owes to happy accidents in the calculation.
steps.cite: T. L. Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics (1921)

steps.label: Legend or history?
steps.text: Eratosthenes' own book, *On the Measurement of the Earth*, is lost. We know his method from a simplified retelling by Cleomedes, written centuries later, which gives 250,000 stades; Strabo and others give 252,000. Syene actually lies a little north of the Tropic and about 3° east of Alexandria, not due south. The story that royal surveyors (*bematists*) paced the 5,000 stades comes from Martianus Capella, writing about 700 years later; Heath called the distance "doubtless taken as a round figure". Some of these errors cancel out.
What happened next

About 150 years later, Posidonius of Rhodes tried again with a star instead of the sun. The bright star Canopus just grazed the horizon at Rhodes but stood higher at Alexandria, by 1/48 of a circle, and he took the distance between them as 5,000 stades.

steps.prompt: Use Posidonius's numbers: an angle of \(\tfrac{1}{48}\) of a circle over 5,000 stades. What circumference does that give?
hints: Same method as before: the whole circle is 48 of those arcs.

mistakes.say: That's Eratosthenes' answer with 1/50. Posidonius's angle was 1/48.

steps.text: Both of Posidonius's inputs were off, and Strabo says he also favoured a much smaller figure, about 180,000 stades. Small estimates stuck. In 1492 Columbus used al-Farghani's figure for the Earth, but read al-Farghani's Arabic miles as shorter Roman miles. He thought the world was only about three-quarters of Eratosthenes' size, which put Asia within sailing reach. It wasn't.
A young mathematician from Perga, Apollonius, comes to Alexandria to study. He will become famous for the curves you get by slicing a cone (*Cutting the cone*).
Echoes today

steps.title: The metre is a piece of the Earth
steps.text: In the 1790s the metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along a meridian: a quarter of the circle Eratosthenes measured. The nautical mile was defined as one minute of latitude (1/60 of a degree).

problem.prompt: If pole to equator is exactly 10,000,000 m, how many kilometres is the whole circle through both poles?
hints: Pole to equator is a quarter of the circle. Convert 10,000,000 m to km first.

mistakes.say: That's one quarter (pole to equator). The whole circle is four quarters.
That's metres. Divide by 1,000 for kilometres.

solution: \(10\,000\,000\) m \(= 10\,000\) km for a quarter circle.
\(4 \times 10\,000 = 40\,000\) km, very close to today's measured 40,008 km.

steps.title: Find your latitude from the noon sun
steps.text: On an equinox (around 20 March or 23 September) sunlight arrives parallel to the equator, and the noon sun stands at \(90° -\) your latitude above the horizon. It's Eratosthenes' idea in reverse: the angle of the sunlight tells you where you are on the curve of the Earth. Sailors used this for centuries. Move yourself around the globe to see why.

problem.prompt: On the equinox, the noon sun in Alexandria stands about 59° above the horizon. What is Alexandria's latitude?
hints: latitude \(= 90° -\) the sun's height at noon.

mistakes.say: That's the sun's height. Latitude is 90° minus it.
Subtract the sun's height from 90°; don't add.

steps.title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes
steps.text: Eratosthenes is also credited with a quick way to list prime numbers: circle the next number still standing, cross out all its multiples, and repeat. Computers still use versions of it, and primes are the basis of the encryption that protects online payments. (The earliest mention is by Nicomachus, about 350 years later.)

problem.prompt: How many prime numbers are there up to 50?
hints: Count the numbers left standing in the sieve above.

mistakes.say: Did you count 1? 1 is not a prime.
